header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, MINGORA BENCH
Sultan Alam Khan and others v. Mst. Samya Begum and others
For Appellants Mr. Muhammad Ikram Khan, Advocate.
For Respondents Malik Muhammad Ajmal Khan & Mr. Asghar Shah, Advocates.
Assistance Mr. Qaiser Abbas, Civil Judge/Former Research Officer, Supreme
body: *** Dr. Khurshid Iqbal, J.- 1. This regular first appeal under section 8 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Enforcement of Women’s Property Rights Act, 2019 (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Act No. XLIV of 2019) (“the Act”) calls into question two orders of the Ombudsperson for Enforcement of Women’s Property Rights, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, dated 15.09.2025 and 24.10.2025. By the first order, the parties proceeded against before the Ombudsperson, were restrained from interfering with the disputed property, and the Deputy Commissioner, Upper Dir, was appointed its Receiver. By the second, the Ombudsperson declined the application of the present appellants seeking dismissal of the complaint as against them. The appeal thus raises, in the first instance, the scope of the statutory right of appeal against orders made before final disposal of a complaint and, thereafter, the limits within which proprietary disputes may be dealt with under the Act.

2. Respondents Nos. 1 to 3 instituted a complaint under section 4 of the Act against seventy persons, the present appellants having been arrayed therein as respondents Nos. 64 to 70. The complainants assert that they, together with certain persons, described in the complaint only as “some of the respondents”, are direct descendants of late Dilaram Khan, son of Sultan Muhammad, son of Ghazan Khan. They trace the family pedigree further to Mullah Ilyas, also known as Akhund Baba, Painda Khel. According to them, Dilaram Khan, who had three wives, left behind three daughters and six sons and owned substantial movable and immovable property situated in different villages of Upper Dir. Their grievance is that they have been deprived of their lawful Shari shares in his estate. The complaint seeks enforcement of those asserted inheritance rights. The precise identity of the respondents whom they acknowledge to be co-heirs, and the correspondence between the properties claimed and the holdings of the various adversaries, are material matters in controversy.

Page 2 of 15 3. In the course of the complaint proceedings, a revenue inquiry was requisitioned and the parties were required to submit their replies. On 15.09.2025, the Ombudsperson restrained interference with the disputed property and appointed the Deputy Commissioner, Upper Dir, as Receiver. The Tehsildar’s report, dated 24.09.2025, was subsequently forwarded by the Deputy Commissioner. These steps are noticed as part of the continuing statutory proceedings; no finding averse to either side is founded upon their sequence.

4. The appellants applied for dismissal of the complaint so far as it concerned them. Their first objection was that they were not related by blood to the complainants and were not descendants of the propositus through whom the complainants claimed. Their second objection was founded upon earlier civil litigation, titled Amir Badshah and others v. Feroz Khan and others, said to have been contested up to the Hon’ble Supreme Court and finally decided in favour of Feroz Khan, the predecessor of the appellants. The appellants accordingly invoked the principle of res judicata and maintained that the complaint could not be employed to reopen title already adjudicated. The Ombudsperson dismissed this application on 24.10.2025, substantially on the reasoning that the present complainants were not parties to the earlier litigation and that no proceedings relating to the property were then pending before a court of law.

5. Mr Muhammad Ikram Khan, learned counsel for the appellants, contended that the complainants had disclosed no genealogical relationship with the appellants, nor any legal foundation for treating property claimed by the latter as part of Dilaram Khan’s estate. He maintained that the prior adjudication of the dispute could not be disregarded; that the appointment of a Receiver over property whose title remained disputed exceeded the jurisdiction conferred by the Act; and that neither impugned order adequately addressed the statutory conditions for the exercise of the Ombudsperson’s powers. He relied upon Falak Shehnaz [(Peshawar High Court (PHC: 2025)].

6. Malik Muhammad Ajmal Khan, learned counsel for the contesting respondents, questioned the maintainability of the appeal. His submission was that both orders were interlocutory, and that section 12 of the Act prevented their challenge before final disposal of the complaint. Reference was made to Ali Asghar (PHC:2026).

7. The appeal presents three connected but distinct questions. The first concerns the reach of section 8, read with section 12: under what threshold may an order made before disposal of a complaint be independently appealed? The second concerns the statutory period for challenging each order. The third, which arises only to the extent whether the appeal is competent, concerns the Mst. Falak Shehnaz and another v. Mst. Farah Deeba and others (PLD 2025 Peshawar 1). Ali Asghar v. Mst. Farkhanda Rani (2026 CLC 1159 [Peshawar]).
Page 3 of 15 lawfulness of the exercise of power under sections 4 to 6. These questions must be answered without determining the ultimate rights of ownership or inheritance, which remain contested.

8. The appeal was instituted on 19.11.2025. The order dated 24.10.2025 was thus challenged after seventeen days, within the forty-five-day period prescribed by section 8. The interval between the order appointing a Receiver on 15.09.2025 and institution of appeal was fifty-six days. Excluding the day of the order, the ordinary period for appealing that determination expired on 30.10.2025; the challenge to it is therefore prima facie eleven days late. The two orders are separate determinations, and an appeal lodged in time against the later order does not, merely for that reason, revive the time for challenging the earlier one. An exclusion of the period requisite for obtaining a certified copy, where legally permissible and proved, would require separate consideration under sections 12 and 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908. In Chairman District Evacuee Trust, the Honourable Supreme Court addressed the application of the exclusion for obtaining copies in proceedings governed by a special enactment. Allah Dino addresses the distinct question whether section 5 may be invoked where special legislation prescribes its own period. Neither authority establishes that an exclusion or condonation operates automatically in this case. Any exclusion of time must rest upon the applicable statutory provision and an established factual foundation. In the absence of a determination allowing such exclusion, the present appeal is examined in relation to the order dated 24.10.2025 without granting independent appellate relief against the order dated 15.09.2025. Sections 8, and 12 provide:
8. Appeal. --- Any person who is aggrieved from an order of Ombudsperson may, within forty-five (45) days of the order, prefer an appeal to the Peshawar High Court.

12. Bar of jurisdiction.--- No Court or other authority shall have jurisdiction- (a) to question the validity of any action taken, or intended to be taken, or order made, or anything or purporting to have been taken, made or done under this Act; or (b) to grant an injunction or stay or to make any interim order in relation to any proceeding before, or anything done or intended to be done or purporting to have been done by, or under the orders or at the instance of the Ombudsperson.

9. The apparent breadth of section 12 cannot be read in isolation from section 8. This is an application of harmonious construction, not a licence to amend either provision. In D.G. Khan Cement , the Hon’ble Supreme Court explained the need to construe provisions of an enactment together in the light of its purpose and the intention manifested by the language employed. Kamaluddin similarly requires the statutory words to be understood as parts of one coherent enactment rather than as provisions defeating one another. The Act itself confers a right of appeal upon a person aggrieved by an order of the Ombudsperson, while section 12 excludes jurisdiction to question acts done under the Act and restrains collateral interlocutory interference. To construe the general bar as Chairman, District Evacuee Trust Committee v. Sharif Ahmad (PLD 1991 SC 246). Allah Dino v. Muhammad Shah (2001 SCMR 286).
D.G. Khan Cement Company Ltd. and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others (2004 SCMR 456, paragraph 18).

Kamaluddin Qureshi v. Ali International Co. (2009 CLD 784, paragraph 10). Page 4 of 15 extinguishing the appeal expressly conferred by section 8 would make that provision ineffective. The distinction between a general provision and one specifically directed to a particular subject is recognised in Qutbuddin and United Bank (SC:2010).

Applying that principle here, the specific appellate jurisdiction created by section 8 operates notwithstanding the general terms of section 12, while the latter continues to regulate challenges outside that statutory appellate channel. This construction gives work to each provision; it does not imply that the High Court possesses unrestricted power to halt or supervise every intermediate step of the Ombudsperson's inquiry.

10. The precise language remains controlling. Section 8 speaks of “any person who is aggrieved from an order”; it neither says “final order”, nor grants an independent appeal against each communication regardless of its effect. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mirza Shaukat explained that the legislative words are the primary guide and that recourse to purpose and harmonious construction is justified where ambiguity or incompatibility between provisions requires resolution. A preamble cannot displace clear substantive language. This Court must, therefore, neither insert the word “final” into section 8, nor convert the term “order” into an unlimited right to challenge notices, adjournments and directions which decide no legal interest. The question is whether the person appealing is aggrieved by a decision having actual legal operation; its nomenclature and the pendency of the principal complaint are not decisive. A direction seeking a report or fixing a hearing is ordinarily procedural. An order transferring management of property to a Receiver, or conclusively deciding a distinct objection bearing upon the statutory forum, has consequences which require a different inquiry.

11. The substantive right of appeal is created by the enactment which confers it; it is neither enlarged, nor restricted by borrowing a procedural rule from another statute. In Deputy Director , the Hon’ble Supreme Court distinguished between incorporation of procedural provisions and the independent statutory source of appeal. Likewise, Kamaluddin examined the language, subject and consequences of the appellate provisions in the Companies Ordinance rather than treating the expression 'order' as unconfined by its legislative setting. These decisions support fidelity to the text and scheme of section 8; neither determines the exact interlocutory threshold for this Act. Mian Sharif Shah illustrates the converse situation in which the special enactment did not confer an appeal at all. It cannot be transposed to erase the express appeal contained in section 8. A. Qutubuddin Khan v. CHEC Millwala Dredging Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. (2014 CLD 824) and United Bank Ltd. v. Mst Jametela Mumtaz and others (2010 SCMR 229).

Mirza Shaukat Baig and others v. Shahid Jamil and others (PLD 2005 SC 530), drawing upon Shahid Nabi Malik v. Chief Election Commissioner (PLD 1997 SC 32), Deputy Director, Regional Directorate, Anti-Narcotics Force, Lahore v. Mst Fazeelat Bibi (PLD 2013 SC 361).
Kamaluddin, supra n. 6.
Mian Sharif Shah v. Nawab Khan (PLD 2011 Peshawar 86).
Page 5 of 15 12. The interpretive approach finds support in the decision of a five-member Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Ghulam Haider.

Although arising under the law of succession and concerning a deeming provision in a different statute, the decision illustrates the necessity of adhering to the enacted words without introducing limitations which those words do not support. The construction of section 8 must therefore begin with the words chosen by the provincial legislature, understood in their statutory setting. The distinction between legal effect and procedural nomenclature is illustrated, on a different appellate provision, by Kundan.

In the family-court context an order could finally dispose of an independent form of statutory protection even while the principal proceedings remained pending. That comparison is persuasive only at the level of identifying substantive legal consequences; the differing words of section 14 of the Family Courts Act, 1964 cannot be treated as if they were incorporated into section 8 of the present Act.

13. Decisions of this Court applying the same Act provide a closer statutory comparison. In Falak Shhenaz , the Ombudsperson had directed the attachment and sealing of property while the principal complaint remained pending. This Court entertained the appeal and examined the legal effect of that interim direction. It distinguished attachment from physical sealing, set aside the latter and maintained the former. The decision is important both for its actual exercise of appellate jurisdiction in relation to a pre-final property order and for its insistence that possession and use of property cannot be curtailed by measures unsupported by the governing law.

14. In its latest judgment in Naheed Shah Afridi , the Honourable Supreme Court held that the Act is, in essence, a law for enforcement of and protection of propriety rights that are already established or readily ascertainable. In Ali Asghar , this Court examined a substantial group of appeals under section 8. Among the matters recited was a challenge to the appointment of a Receiver during the pendency of a complaint. The Court explained that the Ombudsperson’s jurisdiction is summary and confined by the Act; intricate disputes of title, contested questions requiring detailed evidence and the separation of shares in unpartitioned joint property cannot be resolved merely by issuing executive directions under sections 4 and 5. It also emphasised the participation of persons whose legal interests would be directly affected. That authority is not a general prohibition against every complaint resisted by an adverse claimant; rather, it directs attention to the true character and evidentiary demands of the dispute.

15. The construction must also respect the purpose and limits of the protective enactment. It provides women an expeditious mechanism against deprivation of Ghulam Haider and others v. Murad through legal representatives and others (PLD 2012 SC 501).
Mst Kundan Mai v. Judge Family Court, Multan and others (2022 MLD 1621). Falak Shehnaz, supra n. 1.
Mst. Naheed Shah Afridi and another v. Muzaffar Shah Afridi and another (C.P.L.A. Nos. 2630 and 2639 of 2026, decided on 29.10.2026).
Ali Asghar, supra n. 2.

Page 6 of 15 property, without making summary process a substitute for determination of every contested question of title. In Mirza Shaukhat Baig , the Hon’ble Supreme Court cautioned against allowing the preamble to override operative words. Abdul Aziz illustrates the bounded principle that a remedial provision ought, where language permits, to be construed to give practical effect to the relief provided. Those principles require section 8 to be useful in a case of genuine legal prejudice but not a means of fragmenting the Ombudsperson's enquiry through appeals from incidental directions. The threshold is consequently to be derived from 'an order' and 'a person aggrieved', understood within the Act, rather than from a general judicial preference for or against interlocutory appeals.

16. The task of identifying an 'order' under section 8 is not answered by calling a determination interlocutory. Interlocutory describes its place within the proceedings; it does not describe the juridical consequence of what has been decided. A direction regulating the next hearing and a direction placing disputed property under an independent officer's control may both precede final adjudication, but they operate upon different legal interests. If the word 'order' were confined to the latter stage alone, the appeal provided by the legislature could be denied precisely where the statutory action has a present impact that the final judgment may not restore.

17. There is, however, an equally important limiting consideration. The Act contemplates a summary mechanism. Its use would be defeated by an appeal against every call for record, adjournment, notice, fixation of a hearing or direction to produce a document. Section 8 confers a remedy upon a person 'aggrieved', not upon one merely dissatisfied with the pace or manner of conducting an inquiry. The quality of the grievance must be measured by an objective legal consequence. An inconvenience, disagreement or speculative fear of an adverse eventual result does not suffice.

18. The appellate court must, therefore, distinguish a procedural step in aid of adjudication from a determination which itself deals with a legally cognisable position. It is not essential that the whole complaint be finally disposed of. A decision may have finality in relation to a separate entitlement or objection even if other questions remain under examination. Conversely, the fact that an application has been formally dismissed does not invariably give it that character: its substance, reasons and real consequences remain controlling.

19. The first inquiry is directed to what the order actually does. It may adjudicate a particular contested entitlement, reject a challenge to the competence of the statutory forum, place a property under control, alter the ability to use or receive its income, or restrict a right which the party could otherwise presently exercise. These acts must be separated from measures which Mirza Shaukat Baig, supra n. 8.
Abdul Aziz Zehri v. Chairman, Selection Committee (1992 SCMR 1078). Page 7 of 15 simply facilitate the eventual determination and have no independent effect upon a protected legal interest.

20. The second inquiry concerns the nature of the prejudice. The statutory description 'aggrieved' must be anchored to an identified right, obligation or essential procedural guarantee, materially and adversely affected by the decision under challenge. The appealability inquiry does not require that the appellant ultimately prove the order unlawful; otherwise jurisdiction would be made to depend upon success on the merits. What matters at the threshold is a real, present and legally material consequence, as opposed to conjecture, formal objection or a complaint of minor inconvenience.

21. The third inquiry concerns the independent operation of the impugned determination. Its effect upon possession, control, income, a discrete statutory protection or the competence of the forum may require immediate appellate examination. It is relevant whether the Ombudsperson can readily reconsider the question and whether later proceedings or an appeal against the ultimate decision would furnish an effective remedy. These considerations go to the substance of the legal effect; they cannot be converted into a free-standing jurisdictional condition not found in section 8.

22. This last distinction requires emphasis. The expression 'an order' cannot be judicially supplemented by a universal condition that prejudice be incapable of later correction in every conceivable circumstance. At the same time, the ready availability of full and effective correction may demonstrate that the asserted grievance is only incidental to continuing proceedings. The Court must apply the statutory terms to the particular decision, not construct an exhaustive procedural code by analogy with the Civil Procedure Code or another special enactment.

23. The resulting threshold for an independent appeal under section 8 is this: an interlocutory determination is appealable when, assessed according to its substance and actual operation, it (i) is an order determining a distinct contested legal question or directly affecting an existing legal position, rather than a mere step in managing the inquiry; and (ii) presently and materially prejudices an identifiable substantive right or essential procedural entitlement of the appellant. Whether the decision operates independently of the eventual result, and whether later correction will provide practical redress, are important indicators in deciding whether those requirements are met. They are not extra cumulative statutory conditions. The limitation period in section 8 remains a separate and indispensable requirement.

24. In applying that threshold, the Court should consider the nature of the interest affected; the order's direct and immediate effect; any conclusive resolution of a discrete question notwithstanding pendency of the complaint; the Ombudsperson's ability to reconsider or remove the prejudice; and the practical adequacy of a challenge at the final stage. No individual consideration, in isolation, establishes appellate jurisdiction. Nor does a contention that the order Page 8 of 15 is unlawful by itself answer the frontal question whether it falls within the statutory right of appeal. This structured inquiry is consistent with the statutory text, the legislative concern for expedition and the judicial treatment of propertyaffecting interlocutory orders.

25. The threshold is not a disguised exercise of judicial review. The High Court exercises appellate authority only because section 8 confers it, and only to the extent the statute permits. Section 12 continues to restrain collateral interruption of the Ombudsperson's proceedings. The threshold must be applied to each impugned order separately; the appealability of a later order cannot, without a legal basis, retrospectively cure expiry of the limitation period governing an earlier and different order.

26. The order dated 15.09.2025 satisfies the substantive threshold for independent appeal. The appointment of a Receiver is not a mere step in the management of a complaint: it has an immediate bearing upon the control, management, enjoyment and possible income of immovable property, while the accompanying restraint affects the conduct of persons claiming rights in it. Falak Shehnaz illustrates that the interim character of such a property-affecting order does not of itself place it outside section 8.

Its substantive appealability, however, is one thing; the institution of an appeal within the prescribed period is another. The latter requirement cannot be overcome solely because the order remains operative. For the reasons stated in paragraph 8, the present appeal does not furnish a basis for setting aside the receivership order itself. The observations concerning its statutory basis, recorded below, are relevant to any lawful reconsideration by the Ombudsperson and do not constitute an adjudication of the merits of a time-barred challenge.

27. The order dated 24.10.2025 falls to be considered separately. The refusal of an application which merely invites the Ombudsperson to terminate a complaint may ordinarily leave every substantial contention open for later consideration. The present application, however, raised the alleged binding effect of earlier civil decrees and the necessity of resort to section 6 if the dispute required intricate adjudication of title and inheritance. Rather than reserving those questions for proper determination upon examination of the underlying judgments and title material, the impugned order appears to have disposed of them on the grounds that the present complainants were not named parties to the earlier suit and that no civil proceedings were then pending. It thus purported to determine a distinct objection concerning prior adjudication and the statutory forum, with present consequences for the proceedings in which the property remained subject to an operative interim arrangement. The threshold for independent appeal under section 8 is met. Since the appeal was instituted seventeen days after that order, the challenge to it is also within time. Whether the appellants’ objections are ultimately well founded is a question of merits, not of appealability.
Falak Shehnaz, supra n.1.

Page 9 of 15 28. Before examining the legality of the impugned directions, the structure of the Act must be understood as a whole. The preamble identifies its purpose as protecting women in their ownership and possession of property against harassment, coercion, force and fraud. Section 3 confers the powers prescribed by the 2019 Act and imports certain specified powers of the Ombudsperson under the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010. Section 4 creates the preliminary and summary procedure where no litigation concerning the property is pending; section 5 permits restoration of ownership or possession upon conclusion of proceedings in accordance with section 4; section 6 commands reference to a competent civil court where intricate adjudication is needed; section 7 makes separate provision for pending litigation. These are complementary parts of a single legislative arrangement. The remedial purpose is relevant, but, as Mirza Shaukat makes clear, the preamble does not authorise departure from the operative provisions. The Act advances women's property rights through the mechanism the legislature selected, not through an unlimited summary jurisdiction. Conversely, recourse to section 6 cannot be required merely because an adversary makes a bare denial: to do so would frustrate the remedy supplied by sections 4 and 5. The task is to give effect to both the summary remedy and its expressly stated jurisdictional boundary.
29. Section 4, which provides the procedure for complaints where no proceedings concerning the property are pending before a court of law, reads as follows:

4. Complaint to the Ombudsperson in case no proceedings in a Court of law are pending. --- (1) Any woman deprived of ownership or possession of her property by any means, may file a complaint to the Ombudsperson if no proceedings in a court of law are pending regarding that property:

Provided that the Ombudsperson, on its own motion or on a complaint filed by any person including a non-governmental organization, may also initiate action under subsection (1) in relation to the ownership or possession of a woman’s property, if no proceedings are pending in a Court in respect of that property. (2) The Ombudsperson shall make a preliminary assessment of the complaint filed under sub-section (1) whereafter he may, if the matter requires further probe or investigation, refer the matter to the concerned Deputy Commissioner, who, after calling the record, if necessary, and issuing notices to the complainant and her adversaries, conduct a summary enquiry and submit a report within fifteen days to the Ombudsperson.
(3) If the matter does not require any detailed probe, investigation or recording of evidence, the Ombudsperson may, after calling any record, if deemed necessary, pass orders under section 5.

(4) The Ombudsperson upon receiving the report under sub-section (2), may further conduct such summary enquiry and call for such record as he may deem fit. (5) The Ombudsperson after confronting the report of the concerned Deputy Commissioner and the conclusion and findings of his own enquiry, shall call upon the complainant and her adversaries to submit objections, whereafter he may conduct a hearing, and pass orders under section 5, preferably within sixty days of receipt of the complaint under sub-section (1).
30. Sections 5(1) and 6, which mark the important division between summary restoration and civil adjudication, provide:
Mirza Shaukat Baig, supra n. 8.

Page 10 of 15 5. Delivery of possession and transfer of ownership of property to women etc.---(1) On conclusion of the proceedings under section 4, if the Ombudsperson finds that the complainant has been illegally deprived of ownership or possession of her property, he shall direct the Deputy Commissioner or a state functionary or any private person to take steps so as to restore or confer possession or title of the property to the complainant, including measures to perfect such title.”

“6. Reference to the Court.---(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 4 and 5, if upon preliminary assessment, or upon receiving the report of the Deputy Commissioner or upon conducting further summary enquiries by the Ombudsperson himself, he comes to the conclusion that the matter requires in-depth enquiry, investigation or detailed recording of evidence or intricate adjudication, he shall formulate a reference along with all the reports and material collected and submit the same to the Civil Court of competent jurisdiction preferably within sixty days of receipt of the complaint under sub-section (1) of section 4.

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, the Civil Court shall entertain the reference under sub-section (1), as a civil suit and proceed further in terms of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) and the relevant rules.

31. The first imperative of section 4(2) is a preliminary assessment of the complaint. It is not a full civil trial, but it does require an intelligible examination of the asserted property, the source of the complainants' rights, the alleged deprivation and the suitability of the summary procedure. Where the matter is referred, section 4(2) requires the Deputy Commissioner to notify the complainant and her adversaries and to submit an inquiry report; subsection (5) then requires the report and the findings of any further inquiry to be confronted to the parties, objections invited and an opportunity of hearing afforded before an order under section 5. The interpretation of these requirements involves the distinction between mandatory safeguards and directory procedural time frames. In Niaz Muhammad the Hon’ble Supreme Court explained that no inflexible rule determines that distinction: the object and scheme of the provision and the consequences attached to non-compliance must be examined. That approach was applied in Apollo where an express procedural consequence under a special banking statute was material to the conclusion that the requirement was obligatory. Here, the duty to make a preliminary assessment and the opportunity to answer adverse material before a final order under section 5 are integral to the prescribed decision-making process; they cannot be treated as optional merely because the Act is intended to be expeditious. By contrast, the fifteen-day period for the Deputy Commissioner's report and the period expressed as “preferably” for ultimate disposal require assessment according to their words and statutory consequences; delay alone has not been made the independent ground of decision in this appeal. Nor does subsection (5), which regulates the stage preceding an order under section 5, automatically prescribe the procedure for every interim direction. An intervening order which immediately prejudices proprietary rights must nevertheless be supported by lawful power, sufficient reasons and fair procedure appropriate to its effect.

32. Section 6 is not a mere invitation to the Ombudsperson to refer difficult cases whenever convenient. Its non-obstante opening expressly operates notwithstanding sections 4 and 5; when, following the statutory assessment, the case requires in-depth inquiry, detailed evidence or intricate adjudication, the Niaz Muhammad Khan v. Mian Fazal Raqeeb (PLD 1974 SC 134).

Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. and others v. Soneri Bank Ltd. (PLD 2012 SC 268. Page 11 of 15 provision states that the Ombudsperson “shall” formulate a reference to a competent civil court. The rule that a specifically framed provision governs the particular situation for which it was enacted, without destroying the operation of a general provision in its proper field, is recognised in Zia-ur-Rahman, and United Bank, and recently in Qutubuddin.

In the present statute the special direction in section 6 controls the continuation of the section 4–5 summary route where the requisite complexity is found. This does not mean that the mere assertion of a title dispute compels a reference; such a reading would allow a person withholding a woman's prima facie clear property entitlement to defeat the Act by denial alone. The Ombudsperson must examine whether the controversy genuinely demands proof of competing chains of title, identification of parcels, detailed genealogical or revenue evidence, or an adjudication of what earlier civil decrees decided and whom they bound. The express non-obstante clause and obligatory referral language must be given their intended effect once that statutory threshold is reached.

33. The dispute described in the present record contains a number of matters requiring that evaluation. The complaint asserts an estate in several villages and traces descent through three generations to the earlier ancestor, Mullah Ilyas or Akhund Baba, Painda Khel. It alleges that Dilaram Khan left three daughters and six sons by three wives. It also acknowledges, without identifying them in the stated passage, that only “some of the respondents” join the complainants in their claimed line of descent. Twelve pages of pedigree tables, beginning with Sultan Muhammad Khan, are said to accompany the complaint, yet the appellants contend that none identifies their predecessors. These are matters for scrutiny against the property descriptions, relevant revenue entries and other title material. A pedigree—without more, cannot establish that every item of property in the possession of every one of seventy respondents—forms part of a particular succession.

34. The appellants’ want of blood relationship with the complainants is not, taken alone, an answer to a complaint under the Act. A woman may seek recovery of her property from a person who is not her relative if the latter unlawfully withholds it. The legally relevant question is whether the particular property belonged to the person through whom the complainants claim and whether an enforceable right has devolved upon them. It would be equally erroneous to infer from their complaint, without examination, that the property held or claimed by the appellants formed part of Dilaram Khan’s estate. The parties’ alleged absence of consanguinity therefore neither establishes nor defeats jurisdiction; its significance depends upon the pleaded sources of title and the identification of the disputed property.

35. The previous litigation requires a separate and more exact inquiry. The appellants assert that Amir Badshah, son of Dilaram Khan through Mst Azam Jana, one of Dilaram Khan’s three wives, litigated against Feroz Khan, The State v. Zia-ur-Rehman and others (PLD 1973 SC 49); United Bank Ltd. v. Mst Jameela Mumtaz (2010 SCMR 229), and Qutubuddin, supra n.7.

Page 12 of 15 predecessor of the appellants, and that the contest terminated in favour of Feroz Khan up to the Hon’ble Supreme Court. The legal effect of the asserted previous adjudication requires examination of the precise subject matter of the suit, the decrees passed, the issues directly and substantially determined, the capacity in which the parties litigated or were represented, and the scope of the ultimate appellate decision. The plea of res judicata cannot be accepted or rejected on the mere title of the earlier suit or the assertion that a particular person was not formally arrayed therein.

36. The effect of a final civil judgment must be assessed by reference to section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the governing law concerning parties claiming under those previously litigating. Conversely, a person cannot be deprived of an otherwise enforceable inheritance right merely because another relative was once party to litigation unless the legal conditions binding that person or the estate are established. The Ombudsperson’s observation that the present complainants were not parties to the earlier suit is therefore not a complete answer to the plea; nor does the appellants’ assertion that the suit was decided by the Hon’ble Supreme Court prove that the present claim is barred. The former decrees and judgments should be obtained and examined, property by property and party by party, before any finding is recorded.

37. The further observation that no litigation was pending at the time of the complaint addresses only one part of the statutory structure. It may have a bearing upon whether the complaint is initiated under section 4 rather than section 7. It does not determine the effect of a previously concluded adjudication. Nor does it answer whether the remaining dispute can be summarily resolved or must be referred to the competent civil court under section 6. A concluded suit and a pending suit are different juridical conditions; the absence of the latter does not erase the former. The second impugned order proceeded on an insufficiently discriminating treatment of these distinct matters.

38. It is important to keep the statutory objections to the continuing complaint distinct from the legality of the earlier receivership order. The latter, being separately appealable only within its own statutory period, is not directly under correction in this disposition. Nevertheless, the Act requires the Ombudsperson, when making any order that continues to affect proprietary interests, to identify the source and permissible limits of the power exercised and to give reasons appropriate to its consequences. The statutory foundation, necessity, scope and safeguards of any continuing receivership must therefore be addressed by the Ombudsperson in accordance with the powers lawfully available. This direction does not annul, suspend or vary the order dated 15.09.2025.

39. A direction appointing a Receiver is distinguishable from the ordinary power to call for records or conduct a summary inquiry. Section 3 of the Act incorporates certain powers provided for by the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010, but such incorporation should not be understood, without an identifiable statutory foundation, as conferring an Page 13 of 15 unqualified power under Order XL of the Code of Civil Procedure. In Arshi , the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in the different setting of ordinary civil proceedings, described receivership as an exceptional and intrusive measure requiring proper evidentiary and legal justification. That judgment does not itself create a power under the present Act. It reinforces the importance of distinguishing protective process from an order capable of displacing possession or management. These observations explain why the issue merits careful consideration before the Ombudsperson; they do not amount to an appellate order setting aside, varying or suspending the receivership dated 15.09.2025.

40. The requirement of lawful authority and fair procedure is consistent with the constitutional protections of property and treatment in accordance with law. In Secretary Housing , the Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court reiterated the obligation of public authorities to exercise conferred powers reasonably, fairly, justly and for the purposes of the enactment, referring to Article 4 of the Constitution and section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The same judgment recognised the centrality of an effective opportunity of hearing before adverse action. The present dispute is governed by its own provincial statute, but the general principle underscores that an administrative direction affecting property must be justified by the authority actually conferred and the process actually followed.

41. The purpose of protecting women from deprivation of property must remain at the forefront of the inquiry. In Ghulam Qasim , the Hon’ble Supreme Court stressed the vesting and protection of lawful inheritance entitlements. More recently, the Hon’ble Federal Constitutional Court in Bibi Amina subjected the purported surrender of female heirs’ proprietary rights through an uncertain compromise to close scrutiny. Neither authority permits a woman to be deprived of an established entitlement through a merely formal objection. Equally, neither dispenses with proof of the identity of the property or authorises the reopening of rights conclusively determined by a competent court. Effective protection of women’s rights and observance of other persons’ proprietary rights are concurrent demands of the law, not competing permissions to ignore it.

42. The Ombudsperson was required to address whether the estate claimed by the complainants was identifiable in relation to the particular holdings of the appellants; what the earlier civil decrees actually determined and whom they bound; and whether the dispute remained susceptible of summary inquiry or required reference under section 6. Section 4(5) also prescribes the confrontation of the inquiry material and findings to the parties at the stage preceding a final order under section 5. Page 14 of 15 and that the complainants had not been named in the earlier suit were insufficient, without examination of the decrees and the legal position of persons claiming under the parties to that suit, to dispose of the antecedent objections. The order dated 24.10.2025 is accordingly unsustainable for failure to engage with material statutory and legal questions. This finding does not depend upon, or effect, the annulment of the earlier receivership order.

43. Nothing said above determines that the complainants have no right of inheritance, that the appellants own the disputed property exclusively, that the earlier litigation conclusively creates a bar of res judicata, or that absence of blood relationship is in itself a defence to a claim under this Act. Those matters require examination of the pleadings, the decrees and the evidence by the competent forum. Equally, the observations on receivership do not establish that its statutory basis is absent; they identify a question which the Ombudsperson must address if its continued operation is considered within the statutory proceedings. The timely appeal against the order dated 24.10.2025 cannot be used as an indirect appeal against the separate order dated 15.09.2025 beyond its limitation period.

44. For these reasons, the appeal is allowed to the extent that it challenges the order dated 24.10.2025, which is set aside. The application submitted by the appellants for dismissal of the complaint, including their objections founded upon the earlier civil litigation and the asserted applicability of section 6 of the Act, is restored for fresh determination by the Ombudsperson in accordance with law. Before deciding that application, the Ombudsperson shall afford the contesting parties an effective opportunity of hearing, examine the relevant judgments and decrees in Amir Badshah and others v. Feroz Khan and others and the material revenue and title record, so far as produced or lawfully requisitioned, and render a speaking order upon the actual issues raised. In particular, the Ombudsperson shall determine whether the nature of the dispute calls for continued proceedings under the summary mechanism or the reference contemplated by section 6. No view is expressed on the ultimate merits of the complaint or on the plea of res judicata.

45. No order setting aside, suspending or varying the receivership order dated 15.09.2025 is made in this appeal; the challenge to that distinct order falls outside the ordinary statutory period, and no exclusion of time has been allowed in this appeal. That order shall not be treated as having been vacated by the present judgment. The Ombudsperson shall, at the earliest appropriate hearing and after giving affected persons an opportunity to be heard, consider in accordance with the powers conferred by the Act whether any continuing protective arrangement, including the receivership, has a sufficient statutory foundation, defined scope and continuing necessity, and shall record reasons for any action that the law permits. The Ombudsperson shall not infer from the present appellate order either a declaration of title in favour of the complainants or a determination of ownership in favour of the appellants. Subject to these Page 15 of 15 observations, the proceedings shall continue strictly in accordance with the Act. Parties shall bear their own costs.
